activity_context.topic_title: Integration by Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions

examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent

feedback.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡4x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
